Assessment of Plate Curator

Shared catalog editing and release control for State Spotter, a live mobile license plate game.

Where the current curator falls short

Plate Curator is the admin dashboard behind State Spotter’s license plate catalog. Today, a teammate can flag a mistake, but a note still leaves the founder to reopen the record, interpret the suggestion, and make the edit. That extra work grows with each contributor.

What a shared draft changes

Take the Alaska Army plate. An Editor proposes a tag correction in a shared batch. The Owner sees the published tag beside the proposed one and can approve that exact revision. Publishing remains a separate Owner action.

The review flow can run alongside the existing curator because the game already loads versioned catalogs from Firebase. Keeping that contract lets the team test delegation in staging while the current publisher serves players.

RecommendationPilot one staging batch with one Editor and one Owner. Expand if the founder spends less time intervening per accepted batch and requests the same number of corrections or fewer.

Current and target architecture

Vercel hosts the shared curation workflow. The installed game still reads Firebase catalogs, and the existing curator remains the production publisher during the pilot.

Why this boundary? The game already reads versioned catalogs from Firebase, and the team already owns a GPU. Moving the shared draft and approval flow to Vercel let us add hosted Tag through AI Gateway and reuse the same release path. The team could offer parallel tagging without buying another GPU. Editors still decide which suggestions are useful, and the Owner decides what ships.

Alaska · rehearsed Editor-to-Owner steps

  1. As Editor, open Demo: Alaska field edits and grouping. Start with the Alaska Army plate or choose another Alaska plate with a genuine tag correction.
  2. Save the edit, check the before-and-after values, and submit the batch.
  3. As Owner in a separate session, approve the same submitted revision. Stop at Publish inspection. The catalog stays at its current version.

Results and success measures

On the same 15 Alaska plates, eight-slot AI Gateway delivered the last tagging result in 13.6 seconds. The single-slot local GPU took 123.6 seconds. Both ran the 26B model and scored similarly against provisional catalog tags (micro-F1 of 0.669 hosted and 0.664 local).

What would justify expansion?

Compare similar batches with the existing process before inviting a second editor.

Founder workload
Track intervention minutes per accepted batch and corrections requested. Expand if intervention falls and corrections hold steady or improve. Record routine Owner approval separately.
Delivery time and integrity
Time the path from first edit to adoption in the staging game. Check each published change against the revision the Owner approved.
Value of hosted tagging
Track billed spend per accepted tag, retries, and editor review time on both routes. Agree on cost and quality thresholds before expanding hosted use.

Known limitations and risks

  • Review access. Confirm the two-account handoff on the release the pilot will use. An unauthorized catalog advance stops the pilot.
  • Player updates. Staging demonstrated the in-app simulator prompt. Check a physical phone and an active trip before promising delivery. Background push was disabled during the rehearsal.
  • Inference availability. Local jobs need the desktop online. Hosted models can hit rate limits. Editors can make a manual correction on either path. Verify the updated worker’s indexes and idle reads before enabling it. Worker rollout checks

Development tooling

ClaudeCodexHerdr

I started by reading the Vercel docs and taking notes on what might help the curator. The first question in my notes was small enough to test: could a Function read the staging catalog using short-lived credentials? That spike gave me a concrete starting point for the migration. Function spike and tests

Once I understood that path, I used Claude and Codex agents through the Herdr app to implement screens and pipeline controls, write regression tests, and help draft this assessment. I chose what to move, kept production publishing with the existing curator, reviewed the code changes, and rehearsed the result as an editor and owner.

In rehearsal, Publish asked for approval and I couldn’t find the control. The fix restored the actions and passed 29 role and click checks. For the AI itself, we tested tags against a fixed set and blind-reviewed research drafts. Five of seven Eve drafts needed correction, which is why the editor decides what to apply.

What I Do Differently

I’d give plate enrichment a smaller job. I tested Eve’s tool loop for research, and the biggest quality gain came from fixing which evidence reached the model. Our text extractor dropped the exact Alaska DMV listings for Caribou and Celebrating the Arts. Once the model received those listings, the desktop rehearsal returned five sourced facts across the two plates.

I’d start with saved references and official issuer pages, use web search for gaps, then make one drafting call and verify each citation before an Editor sees the result. I’d bring Eve back for research that genuinely needs several rounds of discovery.

One measured Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite call cost $0.00064, or about $0.06 in model usage per 100 comparable calls. The hosted trial required a $0.20 reservation per call. After the first charge, another reservation would have exceeded the campaign cap. That made tighter cost accounting and fewer orchestration steps a better investment for this workflow.

At that model rate, 100 plates with one drafting call and one to three paid searches each would cost an estimated $0.16–$0.36 with Serper or $0.56–$1.56 with Brave, before free search credits. Plates with usable saved evidence can skip that search cost.

What survived the redeploy, and how did the game recover?

A waiting Publish survived a deployment change

On November 16 the workflow received approval on app release 3 at 17:11 UTC. After the deployment alias moved, release 4 accepted the Publish request at 17:29:03 (HTTP 202). The waiting workflow resumed on release 3 and finished at 17:29:10. The request log identifies the receiving deployment, and the workflow events identify the deployment that actually finished the work.

PR #84 · insights/evidence/hosted-publish-v13-provenance.json

One plate made the round trip on the staging game

On app release 8 (5415a90), the Colorado U.S. Army motorcycle plate began on catalog v14 with 12 tags in the Army family. In v15 it gained the motorcycle tag and moved to the Standard family. The simulator was closed during that publish and loaded v15 after launch. A second reviewed publish, v16, restored the 12 tags and Army family. The running simulator displayed the in-app catalog prompt within nine seconds of that commit, then loaded the restored values. The rehearsal drove the hosted API. OS push was disabled and physical-device delivery remains a pilot check.

Issue #135 · insights/evidence/rehearsal-135/RESULT-135.md

The release controls evolved after that rehearsal

The v14–v16 rehearsal documents the earlier approval flow. At the indexed main commit, an emulator test exercises an Owner confirming the current draft directly. An intervening edit requires the Owner to confirm the latest revision. Separate cases check retry after upload, a changed catalog pointer, and pointer advancement committed with its receipt. Those tests describe current code. The recorded simulator run belongs to the earlier build.

Owner confirmation and retries · Snapshot and receipt scenarios

How fair was the model comparison, and where did it fail?
Models and comparison runs

The chart pairs local gemma4:26b with hosted google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it. The usual local 12B model completed 14 of 15 plates in 70.7 seconds. One job expired. A separate paid-tier hosted run configured for 16 concurrent jobs finished 15 of 15 in 14.5 seconds. All results came from the same 15-plate fixture. The benchmark batch stayed unsubmitted.

How reliable were the reference tags?

The v12 fixture used 15 Alaska and 15 Alabama plates. Both states were still being curated, so a plausible extra tag could score as a false positive. The first run recorded F1 0.629 with two failed plates. A later run allowed a retry, completed all 30 and scored 0.640. The 0.600 threshold was calibrated using the first result. A separately reviewed reference set would support a stronger quality claim.

First run · Repeat run · insights/evidence/tag-evaluation-summary.json

Did a more selective prompt improve tag quality?

With warmed local Gemma 4 12B at concurrency 1, both versions finished the same 30 plates. Mean tags per plate fell from 10.87 to 9.67. Precision rose from 0.669 to 0.679, but recall fell from 0.628 to 0.568 and F1 from 0.648 to 0.619. Output changed on 29 plates. The branch also changed vocabulary and evidence normalization, so the difference cannot be attributed to wording alone.

insights/evidence/prompt-compare-2026-11-16/coordinator-report.txt

Where did concurrency stop helping?

In a separate 30-plate adapter test, local Gemma 4 12B finished 28 plates in 83.6 s with one slot and 29 in 40.0 s with four. Hosted Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite finished 11/30 with one slot and recorded 38 rate-limit responses. At 4, 8 and 16 slots it finished zero plates and recorded 60 rate-limit responses per run. These runs explain why completion rate belongs beside elapsed time and why the successful hosted Gemma configuration matters.

What happens when two people edit the same plate?

Concurrent edits and late results

The shared-batch review at 2fb2058 classified 12 of 18 acceptance items as proven by executable coverage, three partial and three requiring staging evidence. Different plates could be edited concurrently. Competing saves to one plate produced a conflict and preserved the proposed value for comparison and reapplication. The two-session component test used a simulated change signal. Separately, job scenarios refuse reports after lease expiry or a plate revision change and acknowledge identical repeated reports without a second write.

Conflict UI · Worker report cases · Firestore execution · evidence/112-115-acceptance-recon-report.md

An older open draft stayed editable after the catalog advanced

On hosted release 9 (9c0c5ee) the game catalog was at v16. Two edits to a v15-based Colorado draft both saved, advancing its batch revision 4 → 5 → 6. Reload preserved the description and accepted tags. A fresh v16-based batch also saved. Both batches remained open and the catalog stayed at v16. On release 10, both browser widths correctly showed the older batch’s before-values as “Catalog v15.”

What changed when the catalog was cached?

Switching states became faster in the local production build

Using staging reads, the sampled state switch took 228–412 ms before caching (typical 235 ms). With server caching alone it took 47–124 ms (typical 60 ms). With the client and server changes together it took 43–77 ms (typical 50 ms). A Maryland revisit took 12 ms with zero new requests. A cold slice still took 634 ms. These are timings from a controlled browser, so the pilot should measure real editors on their own connections.
